title: Crime Indicators and Police-Organization Media Visibility in Canada: A Longitudinal Time-Series Analysis
content: Agenda-setting research emphasizes the role of media visibility in shaping public attention, but longitudinal relationships between recorded crime and media reporting require methods that account for temporal dependence. This study examined national and municipal crime indicators alongside annual Canadian Newsstream mentions of the RCMP, Vancouver Police, and Toronto Police. The national series covered 1969–2023, while the Vancouver and Toronto analyses covered 2002–2023. Initial level-based regressions exhibited severe positive residual autocorrelation. The analysis was therefore repeated using annual first differences, Newey–West standard errors, and AR(1) sensitivity models. After accounting for temporal dependence, none of the national or municipal crime indicators demonstrated a statistically significant and robust association with annual changes in the corresponding media-mention series. The results do not establish that crime rates predict police-related media visibility or that the observed media counts influence public perceptions. Instead, they demonstrate how shared trends and serial dependence can produce misleading relationships in longitudinal media analyses. Interpretation is further limited because organizational mentions do not fully capture crime reporting, and Canadian Newsstream’s archival composition may vary across years.
